subject: Titan Fastener Supply — Invoice #TF-88231 dispute
snippet: Aditi, Flagging invoice TF-88231 from Titan Fastener Supply before I schedule it for payment — I don't think we should pay it as billed. The invoice is for $18,400 covering the Jun
body_text:
Aditi,

Flagging invoice TF-88231 from Titan Fastener Supply before I schedule it for payment — I don't think we should pay it as billed.

The invoice is for $18,400 covering the June fastener order (PO-4471, the M8 socket-head cap screws and locknuts for the Meridian line). The PO total was $14,900. The difference is a $3,500 line item labeled "Expedited Freight — Rail to Air Conversion" that nobody on our side approved. I pulled the PO and the original order confirmation email from Owen Marsh at Titan from back in May, and neither one mentions expedited shipping. Miles checked the receiving log too — the parts arrived on the originally quoted date, June 18, not early, so there's no obvious reason we'd have paid a premium to get them faster.

For context, we've paid four invoices from Titan since January and this is the first one with a freight surcharge we didn't request — the March and April invoices for similar order sizes came in at $11,200 and $13,650 respectively with no freight line at all, which is part of why this one stood out enough to flag rather than just processing it on autopilot.

I called their AP line Thursday and got a "someone will call you back" — no callback yet. I don't want to just short-pay it without your sign-off since Titan's been a decent vendor otherwise and I don't want to create a mess right before the Meridian line ramps up. Miles also double-checked the receiving report against the packing slip that came with the shipment, and the packing slip itself doesn't mention any freight upcharge either — it just shows standard ground carrier tracking, which makes me think this might be a billing-system error on their end rather than a deliberate charge, but I'd still rather get an explanation than assume good faith and pay it.

A few options as I see it:
1. Pay the PO amount ($14,900) now and dispute the $3,500 separately.
2. Hold the whole invoice until Titan explains the freight charge.
3. Pay it in full now and claw it back later if they can't justify it.

I lean toward option 1 — it keeps us current on the part we agree we owe, and it's the amount that actually matches what we ordered. But I know Derek's team leans on Titan for the Meridian rollout, so wanted your read before I do anything that could look like we're stiffing them.

Invoice and the May order confirmation are attached. Their due date is July 5, so there's some runway, but not a ton.

Thanks,
Ilya

body_text:

Quick flag from fieldwork this week. Happy to hop on a call, but wanted to get this in front of you and Karen in writing first since it could be a book-to-book adjustment depending on where we land.

Best,
Nadia

subject: Re: Inventory obsolescence reserve — testing exception
snippet: All, Thanks Miles, that's helpful and I agree with the item-level math on the wheel hub casting. But I want to walk through why I don't think we can treat this as an isolated $65.8
body_text:
All,

Thanks Miles, that's helpful and I agree with the item-level math on the wheel hub casting. But I want to walk through why I don't think we can treat this as an isolated $65.8K correction and stop there.

The wheel hub casting is one SKU in a broader family of Gen 1 AGV components that were discontinued in the same 2024 product transition. When we widened our sample this week to look at the other Gen 1-era parts in inventory — not just the three SKUs from the original testing — we found six additional SKUs with the same characteristics: zero movement in 12+ months, no warranty hold, still carried at the flat 15% rate. Combined book value across those six is roughly $612K.

If we apply the same aging logic Miles used on the wheel hub casting consistently across that population, we're looking at something closer to a $340K total incremental reserve, not $65.8K. I recognize that's a much bigger number and I want to be transparent about how we got there rather than spring it on you at the end of fieldwork.

A few things I'd want to understand before we finalize a position: (1) is there a documented policy for how Northwind ages out discontinued product lines, or has this been case-by-case; (2) do any of these six SKUs have a plausible future use we're not capturing (spare parts program, a customer with older-generation units still in the field); and (3) if the answer to #2 is no for most of them, I think we need a written accounting policy memo on inventory reserve methodology so this doesn't recur every audit cycle.

I know this changes the shape of the conversation from where we started. Given where we are in the interim review timeline, I'd like to get aligned on an approach in the next couple of weeks if possible — happy to set up time with you and Sam.

One more thing worth mentioning: our testing approach here was a targeted extension rather than a full statistical sample, so I want to be upfront that $340K is our best estimate based on applying a consistent methodology to the population we identified, not a precise number derived from testing every unit. If Northwind has better information than we do about expected future use for any of these SKUs — service parts commitments, a specific customer still running Gen 1 units under a support contract, anything like that — that would change our view SKU by SKU, and I'd rather factor that in now than have it come up as a disagreement after we've drafted language. It's also worth noting that this is very similar in shape to a finding we raised with another hardware client last cycle, where the root cause ended up being exactly what I suspect is happening here: a product transition that outpaced the reserve policy update. If it's useful, I can share (anonymized) how that one was ultimately resolved once we're on the call.

Best,
Nadia

meta.action_summary: Respond to the auditor's proposal to extrapolate the reserve correction to $340K across the broader Gen 1 inventory population.

CFO DIVE DAILY BRIEFING
July 15, 2026

TOP STORIES

1. Fed holds rates steady, but the language shifts
The Federal Reserve left the federal funds rate unchanged at its June meeting for the third consecutive time, but minutes released this week show a more divided committee than markets expected. Several regional bank presidents pushed for signaling a September cut; others want to see two more inflation prints before committing. For finance teams sitting on variable-rate credit facilities, the takeaway is simple: don't bank on relief before Q4, and stress-test your interest expense line accordingly.

2. Working capital software spend up 22% YoY among mid-market manufacturers
A new survey from the Association for Financial Professionals found mid-market manufacturers increased spend on AP/AR automation tools by 22% year over year, with the biggest driver cited as reducing days sales outstanding amid slower customer payment cycles. NetSuite, Bill.com, and Ramp were the three most-cited platforms among respondents, and nearly a third said they'd added a second AP-automation tool specifically to catch invoice fraud after a rise in vendor-impersonation attempts.

3. SEC signals more scrutiny on non-GAAP adjustments
The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance issued new comment letter guidance this week focused on companies that exclude 'recurring' restructuring charges from adjusted EBITDA more than once in a rolling two-year period. Private companies preparing for eventual audits or a sale process should take note — auditors are already tightening scrutiny on similar adjustments in quality-of-earnings work.

4. Credit facility amendments: what banks are asking for now
As commercial banks tighten underwriting standards heading into year-end, several regional lenders tell CFO Dive they're now requiring more frequent covenant reporting — monthly instead of quarterly — for facilities under $25M. If you're mid-renewal on a credit line, expect your relationship manager to ask for more, not less, documentation than last cycle.

snippet: Ruth, Miles, Ilya — Pulling this together so we have one clean summary before I finalize the July numbers and before this needs to go in front of Sam if it keeps trending this dire
body_text:
Ruth, Miles, Ilya —

Pulling this together so we have one clean summary before I finalize the July numbers and before this needs to go in front of Sam if it keeps trending this direction.

Total Q2 unfavorable COGS variance on the AGV-200 chassis line: approximately $187,000 against standard, across roughly 445 units produced in the quarter. Breaking that down by driver:

1) Servo motor pricing (Dynatech Componentry) — the SM-40 unit price moved from $286 to $312 without a documented PO amendment, a $26/unit increase. Across all units using that component this quarter (chassis assembly plus two other product lines that share the part), that's roughly $61,000 of the total variance. Ilya is following up with Dynatech's rep both on the retroactive amount already paid and on getting this properly documented going forward so it doesn't happen again without visibility.

2) Scrap rate on the gripper subassembly — up from 3.0% to 6.2% since March, tied to a tolerance change from one of our pneumatic fitting suppliers. At current volumes that's adding roughly $54,000 in scrapped material and rework labor for the quarter. Ruth's team is working a corrective action with the supplier.

3) The remaining approximately $72,000 doesn't trace to a single root cause as cleanly — it's a mix of smaller component price creep across about a dozen line items (nothing individually over 3%) and some labor efficiency loss that Ruth's team attributes to two new hires still ramping on the assembly line who started in May.

For the close, I'm booking the full $187K as unfavorable COGS variance for Q2 rather than trying to split it into "one-time" vs. "structural" buckets — I don't think we have enough certainty yet on the servo motor pricing to call that temporary, and I'd rather be conservative given the auditors are already in the building this month for other things.

Ruth — can you put together a short corrective action plan I can reference if this comes up with Sam or the board? Specifically want to know: (a) timeline to resolve the scrap issue, (b) whether we're going to push back harder on Dynatech or just eat the increase, and (c) whether the new-hire ramp issue resolves itself by Q3 or needs a training intervention.

Appreciate everyone digging into this fast — this kind of variance compounds quickly if it sits for a quarter or two unexamined.

One more data point for context: this is the first quarter since we brought the AGV-200 line fully in-house last year that we've seen a variance this size, so I don't think it reflects a structural problem with the standard cost table itself — more that two independent issues (a vendor that quietly raised prices and a supplier tolerance change) happened to land in the same quarter. Still worth tightening our process so a vendor price change can't flow through four invoice cycles without someone catching it — Ilya, once the Dynatech situation is resolved, can you and I talk about adding a quarterly spot-check on our top ten COGS-driving vendors against the standard cost table? Doesn't need to be elaborate, just enough that we'd catch a 9% price move in the first invoice instead of the fourth.

Aditi

subject: Payroll trends: what 50,000 small businesses taught us in H1
snippet: Hi Aditi, Every six months we pull anonymized data from the 50,000+ small and mid-size businesses running payroll on Gusto and publish what we're seeing. Here's the H1 2026 edition
body_text:
Hi Aditi,

Every six months we pull anonymized data from the 50,000+ small and mid-size businesses running payroll on Gusto and publish what we're seeing. Here's the H1 2026 edition, with a few things that might be relevant to a hardware company like Northwind heading into budget season.

1. Average pay increases have cooled. Median merit increase across our book fell from 4.1% in H1 2025 to 3.4% in H1 2026, the third straight half-year of deceleration. Manufacturing and hardware specifically are running slightly below that at 3.1%, likely reflecting tighter capital markets for hardware-heavy startups.

2. Benefits costs keep climbing faster than wages. Median employer health premium per employee per month is up 9.8% year over year, the steepest increase we've tracked since we started this report in 2019. Companies under 100 employees are absorbing more of that increase than larger companies, since they have less negotiating leverage with carriers.

3. Time-to-fill for skilled technical roles (mechanical engineers, embedded systems, robotics technicians) is averaging 54 days, up from 41 days a year ago. Companies that widened their remote-eligible postings filled roles about 18 days faster on average.

4. Voluntary turnover ticked down to 11.2% annualized, the lowest we've measured since 2021 -- consistent with a cooler overall labor market giving employees fewer reasons to jump.

5. R&D tax credit claims are up sharply among hardware and robotics companies specifically -- 38% of eligible companies in that category claimed the federal credit in their most recent filing, versus 22% two years ago. If you haven't run the numbers on this for Northwind, it's worth 20 minutes with your tax accountant; the credit can offset payroll tax liability directly for pre-profitability companies.

6. Contractor and 1099 usage is up 14% year over year across our book, concentrated in engineering and design roles rather than administrative functions. We think this reflects companies wanting flexibility while capital markets stay uncertain -- easier to scale a contractor relationship up or down than a full-time headcount plan. Worth noting for anyone doing worker classification reviews: state auditors have gotten more aggressive about misclassification enforcement in this same window, so document the independent-contractor factors carefully if your mix is shifting.

7. Multi-state payroll complexity keeps climbing. The average company on our platform now runs payroll across 3.4 states, up from 2.6 three years ago, largely driven by remote hiring. Each additional state adds an average of 40 minutes per pay period in registration and filing overhead until it's automated, which is the single most common reason companies our size cite for finally moving off manual multi-state filing.

We'll publish the H2 numbers in January. As always, methodology and the full data set (anonymized, aggregated) are available on request if you want to compare Northwind's numbers against the cohort directly.

Take care,
The Gusto Research Team

snippet: Sam, Before department inputs start rolling in, I want to align with you on the top-level assumptions I'm planning to use for the FY27 model, since these will shape everything unde
body_text:
Sam,

Before department inputs start rolling in, I want to align with you on the top-level assumptions I'm planning to use for the FY27 model, since these will shape everything under them.

**Revenue.** Base case assumes we hold current customer ARR flat plus 12% net expansion from existing accounts (Vantage Foundries and Tarrow-scale customers upgrading tiers), plus $1.8M in new logo revenue based on Derek's current pipeline coverage of 3.2x quota. I'm deliberately not baking in the two enterprise deals still in legal review — if either closes it's upside, not baseline.

**Gross margin.** Modeling 42.5%, a full point above FY26's blended 41.2%, driven by the Peabody line automation project reducing freight and labor cost per unit if it gets funded in the capex plan. If that project doesn't get greenlit, margin assumption drops back to 41.5%.

**Headcount.** Planning for 12 net new hires across the year, weighted toward engineering (5) and sales (4), with the rest split across ops and G&A. Fully-loaded cost per hire averaging $142K based on this year's actuals. This is the single biggest lever in the model — every 2 hires we add or cut moves burn by roughly $24K/month.

**Cash and runway.** Starting cash of $2.31M (July 31 actual) plus whatever we draw on the renewed credit facility — I'm in the middle of negotiating better terms with Harborline, aiming to close by August 31. Base case burn under these assumptions runs about $165K/month, which gets us to roughly 16 months of runway without a new raise, assuming the facility renews as expected.

**Capex.** $340K planned, almost entirely the Peabody automation project ($280K) plus normal IT refresh ($60K). This is the one line I think deserves real debate before we lock it — it's a big number for a company our size and I want Ruth's ROI case in writing before it goes in the base case rather than a stretch scenario.

Timeline: department inputs due August 14, first consolidated draft August 21, group review August 24-25. I'll have the first full model in your inbox by August 3rd — sorry, meant August 21st, fixing that typo before anyone holds me to the wrong date. Let me know if any of these top-level assumptions don't match your read before I lock them in as the base case for everyone else's inputs.

One more thing worth flagging now rather than in week three: last year's model fell apart a bit at the review stage because each department was implicitly assuming a different revenue number when they built their own headcount and spend requests. I'd like to send everyone the same top-level revenue and margin assumptions above before they start their own inputs, specifically so Derek's sales hiring plan and Ruth's capex request are both built against the same base case rather than three different optimistic versions of the year. If you're fine with the assumptions as I've laid them out, I'll send this same memo to Karen, Derek, Ruth, and Hannah on Monday as the starting point for their submissions, and note explicitly that anything they want to flex above this baseline needs a one-line justification I can defend to the board.

Aditi

snippet: Sam, Wanted to get this in front of you before I respond to Frank at Harborline. They've come back with better terms on extending our $2.5M revolving credit facility, and I think w
body_text:
Sam,

Wanted to get this in front of you before I respond to Frank at Harborline. They've come back with better terms on extending our $2.5M revolving credit facility, and I think we should sign.

The headline changes: the rate drops from SOFR + 2.75% to SOFR + 2.50%, which at current SOFR (~5.3%) saves us roughly $6,250 a year on the facility's average draw, and the minimum liquidity covenant relaxes from $500K to $350K, which gives us more breathing room if we draw the line down during a working-capital-heavy quarter. The facility limit stays at $2.5M and the new maturity pushes out to September 2028, so we'd have another two years of certainty on the line before we have to renegotiate again.

Why this matters right now: we're heading into a Q4 inventory build to support the pipeline of TitanWorks-scale deals Derek's team is working, and those deals come with real upfront component costs before we see the cash from delivery milestones. Having this facility renewed on better terms, rather than scrambling to negotiate it under time pressure closer to the September 1 expiration, gives us a clean working capital cushion without having to touch the operating cash balance we're holding for payroll and the audit-related spend coming this fall.

I don't see a real downside here — the covenant relief is strictly easier than what we have today, and we're not taking on any new debt, just extending existing capacity on better pricing. I'd recommend we sign the commitment letter and I'll get it back to Frank before the August 15 deadline he's given us.

One thing I do want to do is give Tomás a heads-up before the board call so Arrowpoint isn't hearing about a new credit agreement for the first time in the deck — I'll send him a short note separately once you've signed off.

For what it's worth, I did consider just letting the current facility run to expiration and renegotiating from scratch closer to September, but Frank was clear that once it lapses we'd be starting a fresh underwriting process rather than a renewal, which usually means slower turnaround and no guarantee we'd see the same pricing given how much tighter commercial lending has gotten for hardware-heavy balance sheets this year. Locking in now, while we have leverage from a clean payment history and improving EBITDA, seems like the better trade even though nothing forces our hand today. The relaxed liquidity covenant also quietly helps our reporting cadence with Frank's team — fewer tight-quarter conversations if a receivable milestone slips a few weeks.

Let me know if you want to talk through any of this before I move forward.

Aditi

snippet: Tomás, Karen, Frank — Here's the full bridge so everyone's looking at the same numbers rather than a summary secondhand. Trailing twelve-month EBITDA as reported (before any addbac
body_text:
Tomás, Karen, Frank —

Here's the full bridge so everyone's looking at the same numbers rather than a summary secondhand.

Trailing twelve-month EBITDA as reported (before any addbacks): $4.82M. Total funded debt as of 6/30: $14.71M. That's a raw Debt/EBITDA of 3.05x, which on its own would trip the 3.0x cap in Section 6.1 of the credit agreement.

Per Section 6.1(b), capitalized internal-use R&D spend is an eligible addback to EBITDA for covenant purposes — this exists specifically because a hardware company like us runs meaningful capitalized engineering spend that GAAP requires we capitalize rather than expense, even though economically it's closer to an operating cost from a cash flow standpoint. Our capitalized R&D for the trailing twelve months is $410K, almost entirely tied to the next-gen AGV controller board redesign that the engineering team has been running since Q4 last year.

Adding that back: adjusted EBITDA becomes $5.23M, and Debt/EBITDA comes down to 2.94x. That's the number I'd use for the compliance certificate, and it's the number Frank's credit committee needs to bless in writing before I file it, since we're using an addback provision that hasn't come up in a certificate before.

For context on the trend: this ratio was 2.41x at year-end and has climbed steadily through the two capex-heavy quarters funding the new automation line and the AGV-300 tooling buildout. Both of those are substantially done as of this quarter, so absent a new debt raise I'd expect the ratio to flatten and start improving again by Q4 as EBITDA continues to grow into the existing debt load rather than the debt load growing further.

Attached is the full bridge workbook with the EBITDA build, the addback detail, and both ratio calculations (with and without the addback) so anyone can check the math. Tomás — happy to walk the board through this at whatever level of detail is useful; my read is it's a real number to flag as "worth watching" but not a crisis, especially with the addback in play.

Frank — let me know as soon as your credit committee signs off on the addback treatment so I can finalize the certificate before the 28th.

One more piece of context in case it's useful for the board conversation: the capex driving this — the automation line and the AGV-300 tooling — is fully funded out of the existing facility, we haven't drawn anything beyond what was already contemplated in this year's plan, and neither project required a separate approval under the agreement's capex basket. So this isn't a case of us running ahead of what the bank already knows about; it's just the timing of the ratio math catching up to spend that was always in the plan. I'd also note our cash balance hasn't moved much despite the capex, since both projects were financed through the existing revolver rather than a draw against the cash cushion, which I think matters more to the credit story than the ratio in isolation.

Aditi

subject: Re: ASC 606 question — TitanWorks multi-element deal
snippet: Miles, Good question, and it's worth walking through carefully since this deal is material — roughly 15% of the quarter. Here's how I'd think about it under ASC 606. The five-step
body_text:
Miles,

Good question, and it's worth walking through carefully since this deal is material — roughly 15% of the quarter. Here's how I'd think about it under ASC 606.

The five-step model starts with identifying the contract and the performance obligations in it. On TitanWorks, I think we have two distinct performance obligations: (1) the six robotic arms themselves, and (2) the two-year service/support contract. They're distinct because TitanWorks can benefit from the hardware on its own (it's functional equipment, not something that only has value bundled with our support), and the support contract is sold and priced separately in the agreement. That means we don't treat this as one combined obligation recognized on a single timeline — we allocate the $640,000 transaction price between the two based on relative standalone selling price, which here is straightforward since the contract itself breaks out $520,000 for hardware and $120,000 for the service piece.

For the hardware ($520,000): this is a point-in-time performance obligation. Revenue gets recognized when control transfers to the customer — typically delivery, but if the contract has a formal customer acceptance clause, that can push recognition to the acceptance date instead of the ship date. This is the part I want you to double check: pull the contract and see whether there's an acceptance testing clause, and if so what triggers it and whether that testing has actually happened. If acceptance hasn't completed, we may need to defer the hardware revenue too, not just the service piece.

For the service contract ($120,000): this is a stand-ready obligation over a 24-month term, so it should be recognized ratably — straight-line unless there's a reason to think the pattern of benefit is uneven, which I don't think applies here. Set up a deferred revenue schedule for it starting whenever the service period actually begins per the contract language.

Given the size of this one, let's make sure whatever we land on is well documented — a short memo with the contract language cited is worth writing now rather than reconstructing it for Nadia's team in September. subject: CFO Dive Daily Briefing: Fed holds rates, manufacturers brace for Q4
snippet: CFO DIVE DAILY BRIEFING — Thursday, July 23, 2026 TOP STORY: Fed holds rates steady at 4.25-4.50%, signals no cuts before Q1 2027 The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate unchan
body_text:
CFO DIVE DAILY BRIEFING — Thursday, July 23, 2026

TOP STORY: Fed holds rates steady at 4.25-4.50%, signals no cuts before Q1 2027
The Federal Reserve held its benchmark rate unchanged for the fourth consecutive meeting, with Chair language suggesting the committee wants two more quarters of cooling inflation data before considering cuts. For finance leaders managing credit facilities, this means budgeting for current borrowing costs through at least early 2027 rather than assuming relief. Several regional banks have already signaled they will hold commercial lending rates flat rather than move ahead of the Fed.

MANUFACTURING: Hardware and robotics startups face tighter venture debt terms
A survey of 40 venture debt providers found average covenant packages have tightened for hardware-heavy borrowers specifically, with more lenders requiring minimum cash runway covenants of 9 months (up from 6) and quarterly board reporting requirements as a condition of the facility. CFOs at pre-Series-C hardware companies report longer diligence timelines as a result -- often 8-10 weeks versus 4-6 for software peers.

BUDGET SEASON: Q4 planning starts earlier this year
Nearly 60% of finance leaders surveyed say they began FY27 budget planning in July this year, up from 44% who started that early last year, citing macro uncertainty as the driver. The most common change: building three scenarios (base, downside, upside) rather than one, and revisiting the downside case monthly through year-end rather than treating it as a one-time exercise.

AUDIT & COMPLIANCE: PCAOB flags rising deficiency rate in smaller audit firms
The PCAOB's latest inspection report found a higher-than-average deficiency rate among audit firms serving companies under $100M in revenue, particularly around revenue recognition testing and related-party disclosures. Boards and audit committees are being encouraged to ask their auditors directly about recent inspection results.

QUICK HITS
- R&D tax credit refund claims are running 6-8 weeks slower than last year at the IRS due to staffing cuts
- Expensify, Ramp, and Brex have all shipped AI-based duplicate-spend detection in the last 60 days
- A growing share of Series A/B companies are moving treasury cash into money-market funds yielding 4.2-4.4% rather than sitting in non-interest-bearing checking
- Insurance brokers report commercial property and casualty renewal rates up 6-9% for manufacturers with on-site assembly or testing operations, the fourth consecutive year of increases in that segment
- A growing number of finance teams are consolidating their vendor stack ahead of year-end, citing both cost control and a desire to reduce the number of systems in scope for SOC 2 and audit testing

DEAL WATCH
Three notable debt and equity raises this week in the industrial and hardware space, all closing on terms roughly 50-75 basis points tighter than a year ago. Bankers we spoke with expect that gap to persist through at least the next two Fed meetings given the current rate guidance.

That's it for today. See you tomorrow.
— The CFO Dive Editorial Team

CFO Dive Daily Briefing

Fed holds rates steady; venture debt tightens for hardware borrowers; budget season starts early.

subject: Northwind Robotics may qualify for $180K+ in R&D tax credits
snippet: Aditi, I'm reaching out because Northwind Robotics is exactly the profile of company that tends to under-claim the federal R&D tax credit -- hardware companies doing genuine engine
body_text:
Aditi,

I'm reaching out because Northwind Robotics is exactly the profile of company that tends to under-claim the federal R&D tax credit -- hardware companies doing genuine engineering work often assume the credit is a software-company thing, and it isn't.

A quick overview of how this works for a company like yours: the federal credit applies to wages for employees doing qualified research (engineers, technicians, and a portion of supervisory time), a portion of supply costs consumed in the R&D process (prototype materials, test units that don't ship), and contract research costs at 65% of the invoiced amount. For a 50-person hardware company with a meaningful engineering team, we typically see credits in the $120,000-$220,000 range on a first-year study, depending on payroll mix and how much of the team's time is genuinely R&D versus production support.

Two things make this particularly relevant right now. First, if Northwind is pre-profitability or has limited income tax liability, the credit can offset payroll tax liability directly (up to $500,000 per year under the qualified small business election) rather than sitting unused until you're profitable. Second, the credit is retroactive -- companies can typically amend the prior three years of returns to claim credits they missed, which for a lot of our hardware clients has meant a meaningful one-time cash benefit on top of the go-forward credit.

We do this exclusively for hardware, robotics, and industrial companies -- it's a different documentation exercise than software R&D credits, since it involves prototype iteration, testing protocols, and physical material costs rather than just engineering time logs. Happy to do a free 20-minute estimate call with no obligation; we'd just need a rough sense of your engineering headcount and total payroll to give you a range.

Let me know if that's useful, and if there's a better person on your team to loop in (I'd guess your tax accountant would want to be part of this conversation too).

For what it's worth, the two most common objections we hear -- and why they usually don't hold up once we look at the actual payroll data -- are worth mentioning up front. The first is 'we're not a tech company, this doesn't apply to us,' which misunderstands the statute: the credit was written around the definition of qualified research (technological in nature, aimed at resolving uncertainty, involving a process of experimentation), not around industry codes. Prototype iteration on a robotics arm qualifies just as cleanly as software R&D, often more cleanly given the physical testing evidence trail. The second objection is 'our CPA already looks at this,' which is usually true but incomplete -- most general-practice CPA firms flag the credit exists without doing the underlying time-tracking and cost-allocation study needed to substantiate a claim that would survive an IRS exam, which is where a specialist firm like ours adds the most value.

snippet: Team, July close is final as of yesterday, and I want to give everyone the same picture before we start FY27 budget season, since the two are related. **July results.** Revenue cam
body_text:
Team,

July close is final as of yesterday, and I want to give everyone the same picture before we start FY27 budget season, since the two are related.

**July results.** Revenue came in at $1.42M against a budget of $1.38M, driven mostly by the Vantage Foundries install landing three weeks earlier than planned. Gross margin was 41.6%, up from June's 41.2% once you strip out the one-time items I flagged to Sam last week. Cash on hand is $2.31M as of July 31, and burn was $187K for the month against a budgeted $210K — mostly timing on the two open engineering reqs that haven't started yet. Nothing in the July numbers changes our runway math: we're still at roughly 14 months at current burn, 11 months if both reqs fill in September as planned.

**Where FY27 budget season starts.** I'm kicking off the FY27 model this week. Timeline: department heads submit inputs by August 14, I build the first consolidated draft by August 21, we review as a group August 24-25, and I need a board-ready number in hand before our next board meeting. That's a tight two and a half weeks, so I'd rather get rough numbers from you on time than perfect numbers late — we can refine in the review sessions.

**What I need from each of you specifically.** Karen — final July actuals and the audit PBC list status, since Nadia's team starts fieldwork August 11 and I want the two processes to not collide. Derek — FY27 sales quota and territory plan, plus your read on the Vantage Foundries expansion opportunity since that alone could move the revenue line by six figures. Ruth — headcount and capex plan for ops, including whether the Peabody line automation project gets greenlit in FY27 or slips again. Hannah — headcount actuals as of July 31 with fully-loaded cost, which I've already asked for separately but flagging here too since it's the backbone of the whole model.

A few principles I'd like us to hold to this cycle: build from actual unit economics rather than growing every line by a flat percentage, flag any assumption that depends on a deal that hasn't closed yet, and keep the model in the shared template so I'm not reconciling five different spreadsheet formats in week three like last year.

I'll circulate the finalized FY27 budget calendar by August 14 with specific review slots for each of you. Questions before then, just grab time on my calendar.

Thanks all — good close, let's keep the momentum into budget season.

Aditi

subject: New T&E and expense policy — effective September 1
snippet: Team, We're rolling out an updated T&E and expense policy effective September 1. Full document is attached, but here's a summary of what's actually changing so nobody gets surprise
body_text:
Team,

We're rolling out an updated T&E and expense policy effective September 1. Full document is attached, but here's a summary of what's actually changing so nobody gets surprised by a rejected report:

Client entertainment: capped at $150 per person for meals with clients or prospects, up from an informal (and inconsistently applied) $100. Above that needs pre-approval — more on that below.

Mileage: reimbursement rate updates to the 2026 IRS standard rate of 70 cents/mile, effective the date of the trip, not the date you submit.

Receipts: now required for anything over $25, down from the old $75 threshold. This is mostly to close a gap the auditors flagged last year — we were reimbursing a lot of sub-$75 items with no documentation at all.

Card categories: Ramp cards now default to the correct GL category based on merchant type, which should cut down on the manual recoding Miles has been doing every close. If a transaction lands in the wrong category, recode it yourself in Ramp rather than waiting for us to catch it at month-end.

Travel booking: anything over $500 (flights, multi-night hotel stays) should be booked through the company travel tool rather than expensed after the fact. This gets us better visibility and, frankly, better rates.

Approval workflow: managers approve up to $1,000 per report; anything above that routes to me automatically. Client entertainment above the new $150/person cap needs pre-approval from me or Karen — just flag the client name and expected total ahead of time rather than asking forgiveness afterward.

This isn't about clamping down for its own sake — it's mostly about closing documentation gaps before the audit and making the receipt/categorization side less painful at month-end. Questions welcome, and I'd rather field them now than have people guessing in October.

A couple of logistics notes: Miles is running two short optional walkthroughs next week (Tuesday 10am and Thursday 3pm, calendar invites coming) for anyone who wants to see the new Ramp categorization flow in practice rather than just read about it. The old policy PDF will stay archived in the finance shared drive for reference, but starting September 1 it's the new version that governs — reports submitted before then under the old thresholds won't be reopened, so there's no need to resubmit anything retroactively. If you're a manager with reports sitting in your approval queue right now, it's worth clearing them out before the 1st just to keep the transition clean rather than mixing old and new rules in the same batch.

Aditi

We're rolling out an updated T&E and expense policy effective September 1. Full document attached. Headlines:

  • Mileage rate: 70 cents/mile (2026 IRS rate)
  • Receipts required over $25 (was $75)

Questions welcome.

Aditi

body_text:
Derek — to make sure I've got the ask right: you want an exception to the $75/person entertainment cap for deals above some threshold, starting with the Vantage Foundries dinner. I'm not going to blanket-exempt enterprise deals — the cap exists because entertainment spend had crept to 1.8% of revenue last year with basically no ceiling, and if I carve out 'big deals' the cap stops meaning anything within a quarter.

What I will do is set up a documented pre-approval process: for opportunities over $100K ARR, a rep can request a one-time cap increase from me or Miles before the dinner happens, with the deal size and expected attendees. Approved in writing, reimbursed normally. That covers the Vantage dinner retroactively too — send me the receipt and I'll approve it under this process.

I'll get you a one-page pre-approval exception process by Friday so reps aren't guessing.

This is a $2.1M pipeline deal. Can we get some kind of carve-out for enterprise deals over a certain size?
>

Aditi
